Patients with coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) have an increased risk of thrombosis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Thrombosis is often attributed to increases in plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and a shut-down of fibrinolysis (blood clot dissolution). Decreased urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), a protease necessary for cell-associated plasmin generation, and increased tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA) and PAI-1 levels have been reported in COVID-19 patients. Because these factors can occur in free and complexed forms with differences in their biological functions, we examined the predictive impact of uPA, tPA, and PAI-1 in their free forms and complexes as a biomarker for COVID-19 severity and the development of ARDS. In this retrospective study of 69 Japanese adults hospitalized with COVID-19 and 20 healthy donors, we found elevated free, non-complexed PAI-1 antigen, low circulating uPA, and uPA/PAI-1 but not tPA/PAI-1 complex levels to be associated with COVID-19 severity and ARDS development. This biomarker profile was typical for patients in the complicated phase. Lack of PAI-1 activity in circulation despite free, non-complexed PAI-1 protein and plasmin/α2anti-plasmin complex correlated with suPAR and sVCAM levels, markers indicating endothelial dysfunction. Furthermore, uPA/PAI-1 complex levels positively correlated with TNFα, a cytokine reported to trigger inflammatory cell death and tissue damage. Those levels also positively correlated with lymphopenia and the pro-inflammatory factors interleukin1β (IL1β), IL6, and C-reactive protein, markers associated with the anti-viral inflammatory response. These findings argue for using uPA and uPA/PAI-1 as novel biomarkers to detect patients at risk of developing severe COVID-19, including ARDS. Introduction Impaired blood clot dissolution (hypofibrinolysis) and hypercoagulation, inflammation, and endotheliopathy contribute to the pathogenesis of coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) ( 1 – 6 ). D-dimers, fibrin fragments generated after fibrin dissolution ( 7 ), have been proposed in various studies to predict COVID-19 disease severity. However, Sridharan et al. reported that D-dimer levels are ineffective as a prognostic marker of COVID-19-associated thrombosis ( 8 ). We showed that Japanese COVID-19 patients presented with low D-dimer levels even in the complicated phase ( 5 ). A low thrombosis incidence and fewer severe cases were reported in Japan compared to other countries globally ( 9 ). As of March 17 th, 2023, the death rate of COVID-19 in Japan and the Western Pacific region is 0.22% and 0.2%, respectively, compared to that in Europe (0.8%), South-East Asia (1.32%), Eastern Mediterranean region (1.5%), Americas (1.54%), and Africa (1.84%) ( covid19.who.int ). The levels of other fibrinolytic factors, including tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), urokinase-type PA (uPA), and one of its main inhibitors called plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and the soluble form of the uPA receptor (suPAR) were found to be altered in COVID-19 patients ( 10 ). Dysregulation of uPA and its receptor system has been implicated in the pathogenesis of pulmonary fibrosis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) ( 10 – 12 ). While these studies indicate that the fibrinolytic system during COVID-19 is altered, they did not consider that all these factors occur not only in their free forms but also in complexes that change their biological functions. The plasminogen-plasmin system, best known for removing fibrin-containing blood clots, controls extracellular matrix degradation and inflammation, the latter due to its ability to activate other proteases and release pro-inflammatory cytokines ( 13 , 14 ). Only a small portion of circulating plasminogen is converted to plasmin. Free plasmin in the blood plasma can be immediately inhibited by α2-antiplasmin (α2AP). Plasmin is activated on fibrin by tPA or urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA) after binding to receptors like uPAR on cell surfaces ( 15 ). Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and PAI-2 can bind tPA or uPA and block their fibrinolytic activity. Inflammation promotes the local release of tPA and PAI-1 from endothelial cells ( 16 ). Elevated PAI-1 levels modulate neutrophil migration in murine models of bacterial infection or abdominal surgery ( 17 – 19 ). Viral infections are associated with elevated circulating PAI-1 levels ( 20 ). Intracellular endothelial PAI-1 impairs endothelial function ( 21 ). Circulating free, relatively unstable active PAI-1 readily converts to the latent or inactive form by binding to PAs or undergoing structural changes or proteolytical cleavage (e.g., by neutrophil elastase) in less than 1h ( 22 – 24 ). Vitronectin binding to PAI-1 stabilizes the active form and extends the lifetime of active inhibitor ( 25 ). uPA, PAI-1, and uPA/PAI-1 complexes are important prognostic factors in metastatic breast cancer ( 26 ). The uPA/PAI-1 complex typically constitutes ~5% of the uPA antigen (total uPA), and elevated levels indicate breast cancer metastasis ( 27 ). Tissue destruction is a common feature of COVID-19-associated ARDS. uPA is involved in the matrix degradation of tissues during inflammation ( 28 ) and tissue fibrosis ( 29 ). Studies also show a relationship between coagulopathy and systemic inflammation ( 30 ). Plasmin controls TNFα and IFNγ expression in macrophages ( 31 , 32 ). TNFα and IFNγ in synergy can trigger inflammatory cell death, tissue damage, and mortality in SARS-CoV2 infection and cytokine shock syndromes ( 33 ). Because fibrinolytic factors can occur in free and complexed forms with differences in their biological functions, we examined the predictive impact of uPA, tPA, and PAI-1 in their free forms and complexes as a prognostic biomarker for COVID-19 severity and the development of ARDS, and determined their association with inflammatory factors.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: COVID-19 pathogenesis, including disease severity, progression, hypofibrinolysis, thrombosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: COVID-19 pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of impaired fibrinolysis, hypercoagulation, inflammation, and endotheliopathy. Thrombosis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are often linked to increased plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and a shutdown of fibrinolysis, alongside decreased urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA) which impairs cell-associated plasmin generation. The plasminogen-plasmin system, crucial for fibrin clot dissolution, extracellular matrix degradation, and inflammation modulation, is dysregulated. PAI-1 and PAI-2 inhibit tPA and uPA fibrinolytic activity, with inflammation promoting their release from endothelial cells. Endothelial dysfunction, indicated by elevated PAI-1, suPAR, and sVCAM levels, is a key component, with pericellular plasmin contributing to the shedding of uPAR and VCAM-1. Urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA) is involved in matrix degradation and tissue fibrosis, with its downregulation impairing plasmin-driven fibrinolysis and clot resolution, leading to lower D-dimer formation. Increased total PAI-1 antigen is positively correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokines such as CRP, IL1β, and IL6, while uPA/PAI-1 complex levels show negative correlations with these markers, also influencing TNFα expression and macrophage migration. Conversely, uPA/PAI-1 complex levels are positively correlated with TNFα, suggesting a complex role in modulating inflammatory responses and tissue damage. Higher uncomplexed PAI-1 is also associated with diabetes, linking metabolic state to fibrinolytic dysregulation in COVID-19.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: In COVID-19 patients, particularly those in the complicated phase, there is a consistent pattern of elevated free, non-complexed PAI-1, and decreased circulating uPA and uPA/PAI-1 complex levels, which are strongly associated with increased disease severity and ARDS development. Inflammatory markers such as CRP, procalcitonin, ferritin, and IL6 are significantly higher in the complicated phase. D-dimer and fibrinogen levels are also elevated in the complicated phase, though D-dimer levels in the Japanese cohort remained below the typical upper limits for Caucasians. Furthermore, suPAR and sVCAM1 levels are higher in uncomplicated COVID-19 patients than healthy controls, reaching their highest in the complicated phase, correlating with disease severity. Total PAI-1 protein levels positively correlate with CRP, IL6, and IL1β, while uPA/PAI-1 complex levels show negative correlations with these inflammatory markers. Uncomplexed PAI-1 levels are correlated with the presence of diabetes, and low uPA/PAI-1 complex levels are associated with hypertension and heart disease, highlighting the impact of comorbidities on these biomarker profiles. PAI-1 activity shows an insignificant trend toward higher levels in healthy Caucasians compared to healthy Japanese subjects.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study revealed significant specificity in biomarker associations with COVID-19 outcomes. Free, non-complexed PAI-1, circulating uPA, and uPA/PAI-1 complex levels were specifically linked to COVID-19 severity and ARDS development, while tPA/PAI-1 complex levels were not. This distinction underscores the importance of considering specific forms and complexes for predictive impact. The PAI-1 activity ELISA kit specifically measures active PAI-1, not latent or complexed forms. Furthermore, tPA serum levels were found to be similar across COVID-19 patients and healthy controls in this Japanese cohort, contrasting with findings in other populations. Plasmin/α2AP complex negatively correlated with uPA/PAI-1 but not tPA/PAI-1 or free uPA, suggesting uPA as the primary generator of plasmin. Non-complexed PAI-1 protein and plasmin/α2AP complex specifically correlated with suPAR and sVCAM, indicating their role as indicators of endothelial dysfunction, rather than PAI-1 activity directly. Inflammatory markers like CRP, IL6, and IL1β increased with severe COVID-19, but TGFβ did not, and total PAI-1 protein correlated positively with these markers but not TGFβ. The uPA/PAI-1 complex, distinct from the tPA-PAI-1 complex, showed an inverse correlation pattern with ARDS and lymphocytes. Ethnical differences in fibrinolytic profiles were observed, with the Japanese cohort exhibiting moderate coagulation activation and hypofibrinolysis, and lower D-dimer levels compared to Caucasians, potentially linked to genetic and lifestyle factors influencing PAI-1 levels and contributing to a lower thrombosis incidence in Asians. Specific comorbidities also showed distinct associations: high uncomplexed PAI-1 correlated with diabetes, whereas low uPA/PAI-1 complex levels were associated with hypertension and heart disease, but not vice-versa.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The primary target population included Japanese adults, both inpatients and outpatients, aged over 18, hospitalized with PCR or rapid antigen-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection at Juntendo University, Tokyo. This cohort was stratified into uncomplicated, complicated, and severely ill groups, and also analyzed in relation to underlying comorbidities such as hypertension, heart disease, and diabetes. Healthy Japanese and European volunteers served as controls for comparative analysis, with specific attention to ethnic differences in fibrinolytic profiles.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The identified biomarkers, including free, non-complexed PAI-1, circulating uPA, and uPA/PAI-1 complexes, are crucial prognostic indicators for detecting patients at risk of developing severe COVID-19 outcomes, such as ARDS, thrombosis, and rapid progression into complicated disease phases (referred to as 'fibrinolysis-sleeper/shutdown' patients). Higher levels of inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin, ferritin, IL6, IL1β), D-dimer, fibrinogen, α2AP, Plasmin/α2AP complex, and total PAI-1 protein are consistently associated with increased disease severity, impaired fibrinolysis, and endothelial dysfunction. Elevated troponin T also indicates a higher risk regardless of disease phase. Specifically, non-complexed PAI-1 protein and plasmin/α2AP complex serve as good indicators of endothelial dysfunction. The unique fibrinolytic profile observed in Japanese patients, characterized by lower PAI-1 and TNFα production, is suggested to offer a protective benefit against severe COVID-19 outcomes and thrombosis. However, the association of higher uncomplexed PAI-1 with diabetes suggests an increased adverse risk related to this comorbidity in COVID-19 patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: These biomarkers offer significant diagnostic utility for stratifying COVID-19 severity, particularly in distinguishing complicated from uncomplicated phases and identifying 'fibrinolysis-sleeper/shutdown' patients at high risk of rapid progression. An adverse risk is indicated by elevated inflammatory and coagulation markers, high non-complexed PAI-1 antigen, and low uPA/PAI-1 complex levels, signifying prognostic risk for severe COVID-19, ARDS, and thrombosis. Specifically, non-complexed PAI-1 protein and plasmin/α2AP complex are reliable indicators of endothelial dysfunction. Conversely, the mild hypofibrinolysis and moderate coagulation activation observed in the Japanese cohort, coupled with specific PAI-1 profiles and potentially lower TNFα production, suggest a protective benefit leading to a lower thrombosis incidence and a less severe disease course in this population.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study strongly advocates for the use of uPA and uPA/PAI-1 complexes as novel and reliable biomarkers for identifying COVID-19 patients at risk of severe outcomes, including ARDS, especially given the reported ineffectiveness of D-dimers as a prognostic marker for thrombosis in some cohorts. While the PAI-1 activity ELISA kit provides specific measurements for active PAI-1, it has a limitation in not detecting latent or complexed forms, highlighting the importance of measuring total PAI-1 antigen. Total PAI-1 protein demonstrated a stronger correlation with inflammatory markers than D-dimers. The plasmin/α2AP complex and non-complexed PAI-1 protein are considered reliable indicators of actual plasmin production, fibrinolysis, and early endothelial dysfunction. However, circulating free uPA alone is not deemed a good or reliable marker for plasminogen activation potential as it did not correlate with the plasmin/α2AP complex.
